name: Pratte's Reef (permit name: Chevron Reef)
place: Dockweiler State Beach / El Segundo, California
year: 2000-2001 built (Phase I fall 2000, 110 bags; Phase II spring 2001, +90 bags); removed 2008-2010 Phase 2 dated 2000 in Blacka et al. (2013, p.117) [R19] vs spring 2001 above: sources disagree. RESOLVED 2026-10-10: the monitoring paper by the reef's monitors gives the second installation as 23-24 April 2001 (90 new bags, +80 % volume, crest widened and made shallower, placed over the Phase I bags) [R28, p.3]; Blacka's 'Phase 2 in 2000' is not supported by that primary text.
type: Submerged artificial surf reef (ASR), sand-filled geotextile bags in a V/chevron layout [R4][R28]
purpose: Surfing — court/permit-mandated legal mitigation for a surf break lost to a 1984 Chevron rock groin [R1][R7]
size: ~200 geotextile bags total, ~1,400-1,600 m3 built volume (vs. ~3,800 m3 / 5,000 yd3 in the original 1997 proposal); crest ~0.9-2.4 m below low-tide sea level (sources disagree) Mead & Borrero (2011, p.3) give 1,350 m3, the smallest MPR ever built, placed very close to shore [R18] (card 1,400-1,600 m3: sources disagree slightly, both kept). Blacka et al. (2013, Table 4.2; A.11): 64 m x 29 m V, depth 3.0 m (MLLW), 50 m from the undisturbed shoreline; Phase 1 design 110 bags of 3.0 x 2.1 x 1.2 m (~12.7 t, 80-90% fill), crest 1.8 m below MLLW; after Phase 2 (+90 bags, +80% volume) apex 0.9 m below MLLW; crest then dropped 1.5 m in a year; seabed scoured to ~4 m depth [R19]. Primary-source values (Borrero & Nelsen 2003): initial installation 110 bags on 22 September 2000, each about 14 tons when filled, 4 x 7 x 10 ft, max 280 ft3 (7.9 m3), filled 80-90 %; depth at the outermost point after the initial installation about -6 ft MLLW (1.83 m below MLLW); after Phase II within 3 ft of MLLW (0.91 m); obtuse 'V' with apex offshore (p.2-3); 'Pratte's only extends 30' (unit not printed, metres by context; p.14); 'approximately 1600 cubic meters of sand contained in 200' bags (p.16) [R28]. 200 bags x 7.9 m3 x 80-90 % fill = 1,264-1,422 m3 (project arithmetic, not a source value). Project-traced Phase I design layout (not the as-built 200-bag reef): 110 bags, area 435.2 m2, bounding box 58.0 x 28.6 m (alongshore x cross-shore), arms 44.7 / 44.4 deg to the V axis, traced by hand on the Skelly design drawing (RWR copy) and cross-checked on Fig. 4 of [R28] [R4][R28][R29]. Blacka's 64 x 29 m [R19] is therefore 10 % longer than this traced outline (58.0 m); its basis is not stated.
cost: $300,000 Chevron construction payment + $200,000-250,000 California Coastal Conservancy grant + $50,000 Surfrider add-on + ~$300,000 anonymous donation for removal; Surfline's cumulative headline figure is $850,000 over 2000-2008 [R1][R4][R7]. Mead & Borrero (2011, p.3): US$300,000 to build (Phase 1 budget only) and removal in 2010 cost more than twice that [R18]. Blacka et al. (2013, p.117-119): build US$550,000 ($300,000 + $250,000); removal US$551,000 (stage 1 budget $285,000; stage 2 $266,000 two years later); 142.5 containers removed, 1 left visible, 42.5 torn or buried [R19]. SOURCES DISAGREE on the build total (US$300,000 Phase 1 only [R18] vs US$550,000 total [R19]) and the removal total (more than US$600,000 [R18] vs US$551,000 [R19]); all kept.
financed_by: Chevron Corporation (construction, as legal mitigation), California Coastal Conservancy (construction top-up), Surfrider Foundation (added funds + anonymous-donor-funded removal) [R1][R4][R7]
motivation: Court/permit-mandated mitigation for loss of the surfable Grand Avenue break, caused by Chevron's 1984 rock groin built to stop beach erosion threatening its El Segundo refinery's offshore oil-pipeline terminal [R1][R7]
contractor: Placed by barge-mounted crane (builder not separately named in sources); removal directed by Coastal Frontiers Corporation, with American Marine Corporation (dive crew) and Morrissey Construction Company (onshore handling/disposal) [R3][R6][R10]
status_now: Removed. Phase I removal fall 2008 (Sept 30-Oct 17, 2008); Phase II removal fall 2010, coinciding with expiry of the original 10-year experimental permit [R1][R3][R6][R9][R10]. First-ever removal of a purpose-built artificial surfing reef [R3][R6][R9][R10]
hover_text: ~200 sand-filled geotextile bags (~1,400-1,600 m3) built 2000-2001 for roughly $550,000-$850,000, funded by Chevron as legal mitigation for a lost surf break; never produced a consistently surfable wave in 8 years and was removed in 2008-2010, the first-ever removal of a purpose-built artificial surfing reef [R1][R7][R6].
design_as_planned: The original 1997 CEQA filing by Surfrider Foundation (via the LA Dept. of Parks & Recreation) described '10-20 large geo-textile fabric bags containing approx. 5,000 cubic yards of sand' [R8]. As engineered by Skelly Engineering, the built design called for a V-shaped (delta/chevron) reef with arms at roughly 45 degrees to the predominant swell, meant to focus and peel incoming waves like a natural point break, cresting close to the low-tide waterline for consistent breaking [R4]. The goal was purely restoring a lost surfing amenity at the Grand Avenue break, not beach nourishment or ecological habitat creation [R4][R1].
as_built_vs_design: Construction proceeded in two funded phases instead of one: 110 bags in fall 2000 (using the initial $300,000 Chevron payment), then ~90 more bags in spring 2001 once the Coastal Conservancy added $200,000-250,000, for roughly 200 bags total [R1][R7]. Even after that expansion, the built reef was far smaller than the 1997 proposal's ~5,000 yd3 (~3,800 m3) target: built volume is reported at only ~1,400-1,600 m3 [R2][R4] — under half the size first proposed, and by Surfrider's own later accounting roughly one-seventh the volume of Mount Maunganui and one-tenth to one-thirtieth the volume of Narrowneck [R7]. Individual bags were also markedly smaller (~8 m3 each) than Narrowneck's containers (140-320 m3 each) [R2]. Chad Nelsen (Surfrider): 'we probably should have said $300,000 is not enough' [R7]. SOURCES DISAGREE on the Phase 2 date: Blacka et al. (2013, p.117) date the 90-bag extension in 2000 [R19]; the card has spring 2001 [R1][R7]. RESOLVED 2026-10-10 for 2001: Borrero & Nelsen (2003) p.3 give the second installation on 23-24 April 2001, 90 bags [R28]. Blacka Table A.11 also: after Phase 2 apex 0.9 m below MLLW and the crest then dropped 1.5 m in a year [R19].
outcome: Wikipedia states the reef 'had very little effect on the surfing conditions at Dockweiler Beach and ... no measurable effect on the shoreline morphology' [R1][R2]. Surfline's 2008 feature: over 'eight plus years, Pratte's Reef was as useless as useless gets' and 'it never produced a consistently surfable wave' [R7]. Diver surveys found bags had moved, sunk, and been buried by sand, with the black polypropylene material visibly deteriorating — 'largely disintegrated' within about two years [R4][R2]. No coastal-protection or ecological benefit is reported in any of the sources listed in References (negative search result of this card, not a sourced statement). The reef was removed over two phases (fall 2008, fall 2010), the first-ever removal of a purpose-built artificial surfing reef [R3][R6][R7][R9][R10].
why_worked_or_failed: Undersized for its budget and site: a $300,000-$550,000 construction budget bought a reef roughly 1/7 the size of Mount Maunganui's and 1/10-1/30 the size of Narrowneck's [R7]. Crest-depth mismatch: on big swells the crest was too deep to trigger breaking, so waves broke outside the reef [R1][R7]. Pre-existing degraded beach: the Chevron groin had already straightened/steepened the beach and buried the original Grand Avenue break in trapped sand, conditions a small mitigation reef could not reverse [R7]. Material/structural failure: sand-filled fabric bags resting on a sandy, mobile seabed with no rigid foundation settled, sank, and were buried, and the polypropylene fabric deteriorated within roughly two years [R4][R2]. Insufficient pre-construction monitoring: Nelsen said more monitoring of sand bars and beach conditions beforehand 'would have told us the reef was too small before we even put it in' [R7].
unexpected_results: No fishing-pressure or ecological side effects are reported for Pratte's Reef in any source found, unlike Narrowneck (Gold Coast), whose geotextile containers were colonized by macro-algae, benthos and pelagic fish and became popular for local (spear-)fishing, diving and snorkeling, though also flagged as vulnerable to vessel/anchor damage as a design risk [R17]. The project's most consequential outcome may have been legal/political: the 1984 mitigation condition Tom Pratte secured is credited by Surfrider as the first case in which the California Coastal Commission formally recognized a surf break as a protectable coastal recreational resource, a precedent Surfrider says later helped protect Trestles from development [R7]. Surfrider itself updated its institutional policy on artificial reefs after this project, moving toward protecting existing surf breaks rather than promising to recreate lost ones: 'I don't think we should ever trade a surf spot for the promise of building something else' (Chad Nelsen) [R7]. No litigation was found in any source listed in References (negative search result of this card, not a sourced statement).
could_be_better: Surfrider's Chad Nelsen (2008 Surfline retrospective): should have told Chevron up front that $300,000 was not enough to build a working reef; more monitoring of sand bars and beach conditions before construction would have revealed the reef was undersized before it was built; more broadly, mitigation itself is often 'a false promise', and protecting existing surf breaks is preferable to engineering replacements after the fact [R7]. Named Surfline commenters (2008): depth/tide design was wrong ('Andrew': should have been 'nearly dry on a negative tide to be legit', not 8 feet deep at zero tide); distance from shore was wrong, though commenters disagreed on direction ('Randy Wright': 'simply too far away from the shore'; Dr. Jose Borrero, quoted elsewhere: 'too small and too close to shore'); cruder/cheaper materials might have worked as well ('prattes is a joke': rocks or 'smashed up cars'); lack of surfer input in the engineering process ('evan') [R7][R4].
relevance_to_israel: Tidal range is the single most transferable engineering lesson: Pratte's Reef's crest depth was wrong for the local tide swing (too deep to break big swells; ~8 ft/2.4 m deep even at zero/low tide per a Surfrider-sourced figure) [R7]. Santa Monica Bay has a mean tidal range of ~1.4-1.7 m [R12], versus Haifa's ~0.3-0.4 m [R13], consistent with the Mediterranean's generally small tides [R11] — a crest depth calibrated for Haifa's ~0.3-0.4 m swing is a much smaller, more predictable engineering target than one spanning ~1.5 m, supporting Lior's thesis that Israel's small tidal range is a structural advantage for reef stability [R15]. Budget-driven undersizing (Nelsen: '$300,000 is not enough' [R7]) is, in this card author's INFERENCE (not a sourced statement), a transferable governance/funding risk, not a site-specific one, relevant to any small pilot reef Israel might build on a limited budget. Material degradation (UV/wave abrasion of polypropylene bags within ~2 years; the 'largely disintegrated within about two years' finding is the diver-survey report in the outcome field [R4][R2]) is a warning for any low-cost geotextile design proposed for the Israeli coast, including Lior's own 'cheap & light materials... for fast deployment and removal' sketch [R15]. Israel has no directly comparable built ASR yet — its only confirmed built geotextile project is the Ashkelon Geotube, a shore-protection structure, not a surf reef [R14]. Tide levels (NOAA CO-OPS Santa Monica 9410840, epoch 1983-2001, relative to MSL): MHHW +0.804, MLLW -0.849, HAT +1.382, LAT -1.469 m, i.e. MHHW - MLLW = 1.653 m [R30]; this is the sourced replacement for the live tide-forecast figure [R12]. Haifa's 0.3-0.4 m [R13] is a web tide-table figure, not a primary source.

videos.title: Pratte's Reef
videos.relevance_evidence: Title is the reef's name and the description names Chevron USA, Surfrider and Tom Pratte. About 13 of the 30 minutes (roughly 14:00-27:00) are the reef itself: its purpose, designer Dave Skelly explaining the planned geotextile-bag chevron layout, and a Tom Pratte tribute. It is a PRE-construction documentary (closing line says the wave 'remains to be seen'); the spoken track contains nothing about the built reef. Earlier frame checks (2026-09-24) found no footage of the actual reef; whether the picture shows plans/animation is not verifiable from the transcript.

segments.what: [this reef] Narrator intro: Surfrider South Bay chapter + Chevron USA, aim of the El Segundo reef (to restore lost surf). Spoken only, no site footage described.
segments.quote: the designers of the El Segundo reef hoped to restore some portion of what has been lost

segments.what: [context, not the reef] 1983 El Nino erosion; Chevron proposes the 900 ft rock groin (jetty) plus about 620,000 cubic ft of sand. This is the structure whose surf damage led to the reef.
segments.quote: chevron proposed installing a 900 foot rock jetty with a renourishment project

segments.what: [context, not the reef] Groin construction recalled by a surf photographer and local surfers; the groin wave breaks only 3-5 times a year, surfable by experts only.
segments.quote: the new wave broke three to five times a year and only the most experienced surfers could ride it

segments.what: [context] Surfrider South Bay chapter, Tom Pratte's surf-impact survey, the Coastal Commission mitigation condition, Chevron versus Surfrider positions on what counts as mitigation.
segments.quote: the only true mitigation is restoration of the surf

segments.what: [this reef] Tom Pratte introduced as the key negotiator and original Surfrider founder; Chevron forced to fund mitigation.
segments.quote: Tom was the original founder of the Surfrider Foundation

segments.what: [this reef] Reef chosen as the mitigation: an underwater breakwater that could create waves and protect the beach.
segments.quote: we can create waves and protect the beach

segments.what: [this reef] Skelly Engineering selected to design, engineer and permit the first artificial surfing reef; designer Dave Skelly (from about 15:06) calls it a submerged breakwater, a simple design to prove the concept.
segments.quote: it's actually a submerged breakwater this project is kind of the dream of every surfer

segments.what: [context, NOT this reef] Archival film of Hoppy Schwartz's 1971 sandbag reef near the Redondo breakwater, which settled into the sand and vanished.
segments.quote: although no waves ever broke on Hoppy's reef the original concept was ahead of its time

segments.what: [this reef] Skelly: engineering is simple, the hard part is permitting (city, state, federal agencies).
segments.quote: the biggest hurdle for this project is actually getting permission to do it

segments.what: [this reef] Skelly explains the design: giant geotextile sand bags, 12-14 tons each, borrowed from river bank-erosion use, life of at least two decades.
segments.quote: my concept is to put out gigantic sand bags a nice bag weighs about 12 to 14 tons

segments.what: [this reef] Skelly on site conditions (10 ft tide range, mobile bottom, waves from different directions), the chevron/V-shaped bag layout for a right and a left, reef set in deeper water, 6-8 ft waves on the reef, sandbar and smaller waves in its lee.
segments.quote: the formation that we're placing these bags in is a chevron shape formation or v-shaped

segments.what: [this reef] Skelly on consulting El Segundo locals; the reef's effect expected to reach only about 100-200 ft either side.
segments.quote: limited to maybe 100 to 200 feet on either side of it in the max

segments.what: [this reef] Interviewees on aims and the future of surf reefs: prove the concept, not a world-class wave; first of its kind.
segments.quote: basically prove the concept that we can go out there and create a surfable wave

segments.what: [this reef] Tribute to Tom Pratte (died of cancer shortly before the agreement); the reef is named for him.

[this reef] Closing: credit to Chevron, the Coastal Commission treats surf breaks as a protected resource; narrator says it remains to be seen whether the reef will make a perfect wave (reef not yet built).
segments.quote: the crest of the perfect wave will ever rise from the waters off El Segundo remains to be seen

videos.date: 2016-04-18 (upload date; content/interviews are contemporaneous with the 1998-2000 project run-up, before construction)
videos.what_it_shows: A ~30-minute documentary about the origin of Pratte's Reef: the 1983-84 El Nino storm damage and Chevron groin construction, Tom Pratte's Coastal Commission mitigation condition, the earlier failed 'Hoppy's Reef' attempt near Redondo Beach, and on-camera interviews with reef designer Dave Skelly (Skelly Engineering) explaining the planned V/chevron-shaped geotextile-bag design, plus commentary from Surfrider/local surfers and a tribute to Tom Pratte (d. 1994). Confirmed to be specifically about this site via its title, description, and content (references the El Segundo/Chevron groin, Dave Skelly, and the Surfrider/Chevron agreement).
key_quotes: [00:14:30] "We settled on Dave Skelly engineering... he was very enthusiastic about the project... would building this reef destroy something the locals value?"
[00:15:21] Dave Skelly: "It's actually a submerged breakwater... this project is kind of the dream of every surfer."

[00:18:36] Dave Skelly, describing the design: "My concept is to put out gigantic sand bags — a nice bag weighs about 12 to 14 tons, that's a rather large bag. Geotextile fabrics... have been used on the Mississippi River to control bank erosion... these bags will last probably at least two decades and possibly longer."

[00:19:04] Dave Skelly: "Construction in the surf zone is really difficult, and out here at El Segundo we have a 10-foot tide range, a mobile bottom, and waves that come from different directions. The formation that we're placing these bags in is a chevron shape formation, or v-shaped, and hopefully that will create a good right break and a good left break."

[00:23:56] Unnamed interviewee, on Tom Pratte: "Tom basically held a big company accountable for the destruction of a wave. The man was definitely ahead of his time, was a visionary — the whole project really is because of his foresight... it's Tom's reef, period."
[00:26:03] Narrator (closing): "An object lesson to see what happens... whether the crest of the perfect wave will ever rise from the waters off El Segundo remains to be seen."

gaps: No single authoritative engineering drawing reconciling the two disputed crest-depth figures (-0.9 m MLLW vs ~2.4 m/8 ft at zero tide) was found [2026-10-10 update, not resolved: Blacka et al. 2013 Table A.11 give Phase 1 design crest 1.8 m below MLLW and apex 0.9 m below MLLW after Phase 2 [R19], consistent with the -0.9 m figure but not with ~2.4 m] UPDATE 2026-10-10 (audit): the primary paper gives about -6 ft MLLW (1.83 m) after Phase I and within 3 ft (0.91 m) after Phase II [R28, p.2-3]; the ~2.4 m / 8 ft 'at zero tide' is a Surfline commenter's remark [R7] and is not supported. Open (HANDOFF J1): the design drawing labels the same 6 ft as '-6 ft MSL' (0.849 m shallower than MLLW) [R29]; the 0.849 m is MLLW relative to MSL at NOAA 9410840 [R30].
